planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil; space 18-30 inches apart for the mature mounded habit to fill in without crowding.

directions: Named Spring Meadow Nursery's 2026 Flowering Shrub of the Year, this compact Japanese spirea pairs purple summer flowers with foliage that opens orange-red in spring before settling into bright yellow, a combination the breeder markets as new for the genus. The low, tidy mound stays under three feet without shearing, making it useful for edging or small-space borders. Once roots are established it tolerates dry spells and draws in pollinators through its extended bloom window. Light shaping after the first flush can encourage a second round of color.
sources: Spring Meadow Nursery — 2026 Flowering Shrub of the Year

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average to dry soil; space 3-4 feet apart and give at least a half day of direct sun to maximize fall color.

directions: Selected as Spring Meadow Nursery's 2027 Landscape Shrub of the Year, this update to the original Kodiak Red bush honeysuckle was bred to hold a deeper, more saturated red leaf color through the whole growing season instead of fading in summer heat. Small clusters of yellow, honeysuckle-type flowers open in summer against the colored foliage and draw bees and butterflies. The rounded, suckering-resistant habit tolerates heat, humidity, and drought once roots are established, and needs no regular pruning beyond an occasional thinning cut. It works well massed on slopes or in rain gardens where little supplemental water is available.
sources: Spring Meadow Nursery — 2027 Landscape Shrub of the Year

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in spring in well-drained soil; space 3 feet apart for good air circulation and continued vigorous rebloom.

directions: Chosen as Spring Meadow Nursery's 2027 Rose of the Year, this landscape rose was bred by Chris Warner and is notable for flowers that shift color as they age, opening yellow and red and maturing toward a hot electric orange, so a single plant shows several hues at once. Glossy, disease-resistant foliage backs the repeat blooms, which continue through the season without deadheading. It reaches finished size quickly from a young plant and tolerates summer heat better than many older landscape roses. A light spring pruning to remove winter dieback is the only routine maintenance it needs.
sources: Spring Meadow Nursery — 2027 Rose of the Year

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained soil; space 3-4 feet apart in full sun to support the heaviest spring and fall flower sets.

directions: Named Spring Meadow Nursery's 2027 Flowering Shrub of the Year, this addition to the Bloomerang reblooming lilac line is marketed as the heaviest rebloomer in the series, carrying fragrant pink-purple flower clusters through a strong spring display and then again from late summer into fall. The compact, rounded habit stays well under most older lilacs' mature size, fitting foundation plantings and smaller borders. Deadheading the spent spring flowers encourages the later flush, though the plant will still rebloom without it. Good air circulation and full sun help keep the foliage free of powdery mildew.
sources: Spring Meadow Nursery — 2027 Flowering Shrub of the Year

planting.note: Move containers outdoors after the last frost once nights stay above 50F; in zones below 9, bring plants indoors or into a greenhouse well before the first fall frost.

directions: Chosen as Spring Meadow Nursery's 2027 Heat Loving Shrub of the Year in the Hollywood Hibiscus line, this tropical hibiscus produces large, flat-faced yellow blooms with a bold red-and-burgundy throat from spring through fall. It thrives in sustained heat and humidity and draws hummingbirds whenever it is in flower. Gardeners outside zones 9-11 can grow it as a patio container specimen, cutting it back and overwintering it indoors before frost. Regular watering during active summer growth keeps bloom production steady.
sources: Spring Meadow Nursery — 2027 Heat Loving Shrub of the Year

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in consistently moist to wet soil; this native buttonbush tolerates standing water and is well suited to rain gardens or pond margins.

directions: This update to the native buttonbush was bred for a noticeably tidier, more compact habit and a much heavier flower set than the species or the original Sugar Shack. Round, fragrant white flower clusters open in summer and are followed by showy red seedheads that persist into fall, feeding both pollinators and birds. Because it is native to wet meadows and pond edges, it is one of the few flowering shrubs that genuinely thrives in soil that stays soggy for extended periods. It needs little pruning beyond removing dead wood in late winter.
sources: Spring Meadow Nursery — Native Species program

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil; space 2-3 feet apart for a low, unsheared hedge or foundation planting.

directions: Developed from the native southeastern evergreen yaupon holly, this dwarf selection naturally forms a dense, rounded mound without the regular clipping that boxwood or sheared yaupon normally require, making it a low-maintenance stand-in for formal hedging. Its small, glossy evergreen leaves give year-round structure to borders and foundation beds. Once established it tolerates heat, humidity, and drought with ease and is rarely browsed by deer. Because it keeps its shape on its own, pruning can be limited to removing the occasional stray shoot.
sources: Spring Meadow Nursery — Native Species program
